source.title: Bending the Scaling Law Curve in Large-Scale Recommendation Systems
source.authors: Qin Ding; Kevin Course; Linjian Ma; Jianhui Sun; Ruo-Chen Liu; Zhao Zhu; Chunxing Yin; Wei Li; Dai Li; Yu Shi; Xuan Cao; Ze Yang; Han Li; Xing Liu; Bi Xue; Hong-Wei Li; Rui Jian; Da He; Jing Qian; Matt Ma; Qun-Shu Zhang; Rui Li

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and figure labels are flattened in the text extraction, but the relevant figure captions and descriptions are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits compute-scaling curves for sequential recommendation models, extending scaling-law analysis to a recommendation setting rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. and assumes a power-law form for normalized entropy as a function of compute. Its own fitted compute-scaling curves for recommendation models are relevant to V5. It does not test language-model pretraining loss, parameter or token scaling, predictions from small runs to much larger runs, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or downstream language-model performance. The production A/B results and system-speed benchmarks do not themselves test these scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study assumes rather than tests that recommendation NE follows a power law in compute. Appendix F states the form L(C)=αC^-β and fixes the irreducible term at zero. The curves are used only to compare its own architectures' exponents (ULTRA-HSTU, SLA, attention truncation vs HSTU). No goodness-of-fit or test against alternative forms is reported. The main text fits straight lines to the same kind of data (Figures 1 and 5). Compute spans well under one order of magnitude (about 10^2 to 10^2.6 GFLOP/item). So the results cannot show whether a power law holds over several orders of magnitude in this domain.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that self-attention beats cross-attention. They find that scaling compute in attention layers and sequence length keeps improving recommendation quality. They report that ULTRA-HSTU's co-design yields about 5× training and 21× inference scaling efficiency (linear-slope basis) and higher fitted power-law exponents than HSTU. They also report deployment with 4–8% engagement and consumption gains.
record.recipe_differences: The study concerns sequential recommendation models and C-NE rather than language-model held-out pretraining loss. It fits compute-only curves and compares architectures; it does not vary parameters and tokens to find compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted compute exponents differ across the HSTU, SLA, attention-truncation, and ULTRA-HSTU configurations.

fits_no_version.finding: In industrial sequential recommenders, C-NE improves monotonically as compute rises via longer sequences and more layers. Table 2 gives HSTU 0 to −0.44% and ULTRA-HSTU 0 to −0.78% C-NE. Tiny power-law exponents (about 0.002–0.01) are fitted over under one decade of compute, and architecture changes alter the exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recommendation-model quality improves with compute, and the compute-scaling slope depends on architecture (attention design, topology).

fits_no_version.finding: Depth scaling saturates for cross-attention by 9 layers (−0.14% C-NE at both 9 and 12 layers). Self-attention keeps improving (−0.46% at 12 layers).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth-scaling returns in recommenders depend on the attention mechanism.

record.peer_reviewed: Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (venue stated in metadata)
record.problems: The analysis explicitly assumes a power-law form for NE as a function of compute and does not report fit uncertainty or a test of extrapolation accuracy. It reports compute scaling only, not parameter or token scaling. The measured metric is normalized entropy for recommendation tasks rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No fitted compute-scaling rows omitted. Other system-efficiency, production A/B, and task-quality comparisons were left out because they do not measure the power-law form of recommendation quality versus compute.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation to larger runs.
All: no fixed-parameter shape comparisons in LMs.
Whether a power-law form holds for recommendation models. The form is assumed, not checked, over under one decade of compute.
All: no comparison of fitting choices. The paper only notes that the L∞=0 assumption biases its exponents.

missing.what: Raw scaling grid: C-NE versus training/inference TFLOP across sequence lengths 3072–16384 and 6–18 layers.
Linear-fit scaling slopes (5.3×/21.4×, 2.7×/5.1×) on similar data, showing that the functional form is not discriminated.

record.verdict_notes: The exponent ratios are internally inconsistent: the text gives 2.08×/4.59×, while the Figure 7 caption and labels give 3.09×/3.52×. The authors themselves describe the power law as an assumption with L∞=0 that underestimates exponents. Minus signs on the exponents are lost in the text extraction.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and their growth with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
The study tests compute-scaling curves in sequential recommendation models only; it does not test image or video model scaling, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream language-model task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Whether published exponents or compute-optimal splits differ due to fitting choices, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus training FLOP.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 7 label gives HSTU, 0.69 C^-0.0022.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a fitted compute scaling law; C-NE is their normalized-entropy recommendation metric.
rows.check: A fitted exponent under an assumed power law (L∞=0) over under one decade of compute. It cannot show whether the power-law form holds. It is the comparator for the authors' method.

rows.subject: ULTRA-HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus training FLOP.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 7 label gives ULTRA-HSTU, 0.71 C^-0.0068.
rows.note: The text reports a 2.08× training-FLOP scaling-exponent improvement over HSTU.
rows.check: This is the authors' method's fitted exponent versus the HSTU baseline. The note's 2.08× (text) conflicts with the caption's 3.09×, which is the ratio of the plotted labels (0.0068/0.0022).

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus inference FLOP.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 7 label gives HSTU, 0.69 C^-0.0017.
rows.note: The authors describe this as a fitted compute scaling law; C-NE is their normalized-entropy recommendation metric.
rows.check: The power law is assumed, not tested, and the compute range is narrow. Comparator row.

rows.subject: ULTRA-HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus inference FLOP.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 7 label gives ULTRA-HSTU, 0.7 C^-0.006.
rows.note: The text reports a 4.59× inference-FLOP scaling-exponent improvement over HSTU.
rows.check: This is the authors' method's exponent. The note's 4.59× (text) conflicts with the caption's 3.52×, which matches the labels (0.006/0.0017).

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus training FLOP in the SLA ablation.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 8 label gives HSTU, 0.7 C^-0.0056.
rows.note: The authors report the SLA comparison as an improvement to the fitted scaling exponent.
rows.check: Ablation comparator under an assumed power law. The power-law form is not tested.

rows.subject: HSTU-SLA
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus training FLOP.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 8 label gives HSTU-SLA, 0.71 C^-0.0078.
rows.note: The text reports a 1.39× improvement to the training scaling exponent versus HSTU.
rows.check: Method-versus-baseline exponent comparison (SLA). Not a test of the power-law form.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus inference FLOP in the SLA ablation.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 8 label gives HSTU, 0.7 C^-0.0059.
rows.note: The authors report the SLA comparison as an improvement to the fitted scaling exponent.
rows.check: Ablation comparator under an assumed power law.

rows.subject: HSTU-SLA
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus inference FLOP.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 8 label gives HSTU-SLA, 0.72 C^-0.01.
rows.note: The text reports a 1.69× improvement to the inference scaling exponent versus HSTU.
rows.check: Method-versus-baseline exponent comparison (SLA, inference). Not a test of the power-law form.

rows.subject: HSTU
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus inference FLOP in the attention-truncation comparison.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 8 label gives HSTU, 0.73 C^-0.0044.
rows.note: The authors report the attention-truncation comparison as an improvement to the fitted inference exponent.
rows.check: Ablation comparator. The compute range is about 10^1.7 to 10^2.4.

rows.subject: AT
rows.operation_detail: Fit a compute-scaling curve for C-NE versus inference FLOP using attention truncation.
rows.measure: Fitted C-NE compute-scaling curve; Figure 8 label gives AT, 0.74 C^-0.0079.
rows.note: The text reports a 1.8× improvement to the inference compute-scaling exponent versus HSTU.
rows.check: Method-versus-baseline exponent comparison (attention truncation). Not a test of the power-law form.

reader_labels.condition: Fitted compute-scaling curves for the tested industrial sequential recommendation models and architecture variants
reader_labels.reason: The authors report fitted C-NE compute-scaling curves and exponent improvements in the recommendation setting (r1-r10); their analysis assumes a power-law form.
